title: Sex-Realist Feminism and Christianity: A Report from the Fairer Disputations Conference
author: Nadya Williams
summary: Williams reports on the Women's Convention in Rochester, New York, convened by Erika Bachiochi and built around the journal Fairer Disputations and its sex-realist feminism. She opens with a pattern among prominent European women writers who concluded that contemporary sexual norms were harming women, proposed alternatives that resembled historic Judeo-Christian mores, and then came to the faith themselves. What surprised her was the convention's reach beyond the journal's readership, drawing health professionals, educators, journalists and many mothers with babies in tow. Her central takeaway is that ideas about men and women take root through in-person friendship and community rather than online discourse, which several speakers blamed for pornography, loneliness and despair among young women. Wendell Berry's refusal to buy a computer, grounded in his working partnership with his wife, becomes her image of refusing to let a machine replace a beloved person. She closes with the convention's answer to what women and men need, joyful in-person friendship and community, rooted in the confidence of God's love.
points: Williams describes a recurring path by which writers such as Louise Perry and Mary Harrington moved from critiquing sexual liberalism to embracing Christianity.
The convention drew far beyond its journal's readership, with so many babies present that bringing a child made her blend in.
Speakers identified pornography and online life as chief drivers of the gender troubles and loneliness facing both sexes.
Berry's refusal to buy a computer is reread as a defense of his collaborative marriage against an intervening machine.
The proposed remedy is embodied community and friendship, summed up in Helen Roy's line that what we need is a party.
quotes: The writer proposed a better way of treating women, then came to realize that what she was proposing was effectively a return to historic Judaeo-Christian sexual mores and the inextricably connected treasuring of women as women and men as men in a world that insists on treating both as interchangeable.

It showed a real possibility of scaling up intellectually honest and deep conversations about gender in our world, and the hunger for these conversations beyond merely the conservative Christian circles.

Indeed, perhaps the key takeaway from the event for me was that while we need publications to begin and foster fruitful conversations, ideas can only fully take root and flourish in individual souls and lives through in-person conversations and relationships.
We are surrounded by more words than ever on our screens, but these can never replace the conversation of friends who gather together with us.
The computer, in other words, is not the problem—but the removal of the need for conversations with a real person is. The result is invariably an erosion of relationships.
Technology offers the illusion of shedding the body or the possibility of changing the body altogether—but these false promises will only destroy and disappoint and isolate.
That was the question of the weekend, and answers invariably came back to the need to foster joyful friendships in person, to build communities, and to reach out to the lonely and suffering around.
